extracted.intended_audience: painters, visual artists, art students, and art instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for painters on the mental habits, education, technical knowledge, and practical conduct that produce high art — emphasizing direct vision over accumulated learning and rules. Advises what knowledge to acquire, how to handle materials and pupils, and what artistic aims to pursue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception over reflective thought
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist must be a perceiving man: receive all things on the broad, white, lucid field of his soul and be open to receive, rather than be a thinking man who, when reflecting, closes his eyes to the external world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid following a single new intellectual discovery so far that you lose sight of other visual facts. Sit still and open your heart to receive multiple, simultaneous sensory impressions; do not let reflection 'close his eyes' to the visible world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep knowledge subordinate to artistic work
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is useful only so long as it is kept utterly, servilely, subordinate to the artist's divine work and trampled under his feet the moment it threatens to entangle him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a piece of learned knowledge begins to set itself in opposition to your sight or to your immediate artistic need, discard or 'disgrace' it forthwith. Use knowledge as a servant, not as master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be educated rather than merely learned
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist need not be a learned man, and often learning is a disadvantage; but he ought to be an educated man — one who understands his uses and duties, is well read in the best books, high-bred in heart and bearing, and fit for the best society while keeping out of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate broad judgement, manners, and understanding of the world (education), without accumulating scholarly detail that cramps imagination and practice (excessive 'learning').

rubrics_metrics.name: Master practical manipulation and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: An artist ought to know thoroughly the whole mystery of manipulation and manufacture: the chemistry of colors and materials, preparing his own colors, and practical manual tasks (color-grinding, canvas-stretching).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the exact empirical recipes and timings (e.g., how many minutes and seconds a powder must be calcined) needed to achieve reliable materials; practical science should be a minor, refreshing subject that does not interfere with higher functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach and transmit technical knowledge to pupils
rubrics_metrics.description: Every great master should have a certain number of pupils to whom he imparts all knowledge of materials and methods so that, by about fifteen, they may know what he knows in these matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work publicly where possible; demonstrate small quotidian practices that cannot be verbalized. Ensure pupils learn material methods early so that they are 'never be troubled about methods any more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Share empirical discoveries publicly
rubrics_metrics.description: All practical discoveries of methods and materials ought to be thrown into the common stock without concealment, to avoid fruitless, uncommunicated experiments and lost processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jealous concealment of methods. If one discovers better materials or methods, make them public forthwith so the body of artists can establish indisputable best practices (e.g., best white, best brown, strongest canvas, safest varnish).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer empirical practice over theoretical speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Artists should work empirically and not embarrass themselves with theories or reasons about things (e.g., whether light moves in rays or waves), focusing on 'how' to produce desired effects rather than abstract physical explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scientific knowledge only as a practical tool (like a microscope) to aid the eye; avoid over-theorizing that does not directly inform technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple, reliable means; avoid fantastical materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The simplest means are enough for a great man; new mixtures and manipulations of exotic materials lead to confusion and distract from 'the one goodness in art' that comes from a rare human hand and soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure a few ordinary colors and a stable white surface first; do not chase novel, cheap, or false substances that blind the artist to enduring truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vision (direct seeing) is essential; knowledge is an aid only
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be done well in art except by vision; scientific principles and accumulated experience are helps to the eye but cannot replace direct sight and feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on humble, unscientific looking at the object. Rules of perspective or aerial perspective cannot substitute for seeing the actual line, color, or gradation in front of you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat accumulated factual knowledge at its true (limited) value
rubrics_metrics.description: Accumulated facts about visible phenomena are valuable only to enable one more quickly and accurately to see for oneself; they should be received 'only at their true value, and an exceedingly small one.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use texts and rules as aids to develop personal sight; do not expect them to make you a true perceiver without practice of seeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of knowledge's conceit and inaccuracy (e.g., aerial perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific knowledge can breed conceit and produce inaccurate conventional effects (the modern exaggeration of aerial perspective) which betray the artist and deaden appreciation of older masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of received technical doctrines; test them against real observation. Do not let a single learned rule cause contempt for great works that employed different or intuitive methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate and measure knowledge like food
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge is mental food: ask whether the knowledge is good and simple, how much will best enable artistic work, and whether it will leave heart and eyes clear. Overconsumption deadens imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquire only the kinds and amounts of knowledge that nourish your artistic purpose. Keep 'daily bread' of practical, digestible knowledge rather than hoarding vast stores that rot or paralyze.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to capture the immeasurable and fleeting
rubrics_metrics.description: The true aim of noble art is to stay what is fleeting and to enlighten what is incomprehensible — to record dim, momentary glances, faint emotion, and those things which are intangible and without duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize representing spirit, emotion, and fleeting sensations over merely measurable external facts or anatomical detail; value perception that immortalizes the unmeasurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit social immersion; be a watcher rather than a companion
rubrics_metrics.description: Society can have a destructive influence on an artist by sympathizing with meaner powers, chilling understanding of greater powers, and occupying time and thoughts; a painter of men must be among men but as a watcher, not a companion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain sufficient distance from social distractions to preserve time, thought, and receptivity for artistic vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hoarding inert knowledge; use stored knowledge actively
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge kept in 'granaries' without being tasted may rot or become useless; many men must receive daily nourishment from knowledge rather than only store it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activate and test acquired knowledge in practice; prioritize knowledge that is 'in order' and within reach when needed, rather than sheer accumulation for prestige.
